chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: 1801—I have just come back from visiting my landlord—the only neighbour I shall have to put up with. This is certainly beautiful country! Nowhere in England, I believe, could I have chosen a place so entirely cut off from the bustle of society. A perfect heaven for a man who hates company—and Mr. Heathcliff and I make an excellent pair to share its desolation. A splendid fellow! He had no idea how warmly I felt towards him when, as I rode up, I saw his black eyes retreat so suspiciously beneath their brows, and when, on hearing my name, his fingers burrowed still deeper into his waistcoat, determined to guard their privacy.
“Mr. Heathcliff?” I asked.
He answered with a nod.

“Mr. Lockwood, sir, your new tenant. I have the honour of paying my respects as soon as I can after arriving, and hope I have not inconvenienced you by asking so persistently to rent Thrushcross Grange: I heard yesterday that you had been considering—”
“Thrushcross Grange belongs to me, sir,” he cut in, with a wince. “I would let nobody inconvenience me if I could prevent it—come in!”

His “come in” emerged through clenched teeth and meant, plainly enough, “Go to the Devil!” Even the gate he leaned on showed no inclination to support the invitation by moving; and I think that decided me to accept it. I was interested in a man who seemed to carry reserve even further than I did myself.

Once he saw my horse's chest actually pressing against the gate, he reached out to unfasten its chain, then led me sullenly up the paved path. As we entered the courtyard he called, “Joseph, take Mr. Lockwood's horse; and bring us some wine.”

“That must be the entire household staff, I suppose,” I reflected on hearing these combined instructions. “No wonder grass grows between the paving stones, and the hedges have only cattle to trim them.”

Joseph was elderly—no, old; very old, perhaps, though vigorous and wiry. “The Lord help us!” he muttered to himself in a low, peevishly disapproving voice as he took my horse. Meanwhile, he gave my face so sour a look that I generously supposed he needed divine assistance to digest his dinner, and that his pious outburst had nothing to do with my unexpected arrival.

Mr. Heathcliff's house is called Wuthering Heights. “Wuthering” is an expressive local word for the atmospheric uproar to which its exposed position subjects it in stormy weather. They must indeed have plenty of fresh, bracing air up there at all times: you can judge the strength of the north wind sweeping over the ridge by the extreme tilt of a few stunted fir trees beside the house, and by a row of gaunt thorns stretching their branches all one way, as though begging the sun for charity. Fortunately, the architect had the foresight to make it solid: the narrow windows are set deep in the walls, and great projecting stones protect the corners.

Before stepping inside, I stopped to admire the fantastic carvings scattered lavishly across the front, particularly round the main doorway. Above it, among a wilderness of crumbling griffins and shameless little boys, I made out the date “1500” and the name “Hareton Earnshaw.” I would have offered a few observations and asked the ill-tempered owner for a brief history of the place; but his stance in the doorway seemed to demand that I either come in immediately or leave altogether. I did not want to try his patience further before inspecting the inner sanctuary.

A single step took us into the family sitting room, without any preliminary hall or passage. Here they call this principal room “the house.” It generally serves as both kitchen and parlour; but at Wuthering Heights I think the kitchen has been driven into a separate part of the building altogether. At any rate, I could hear voices chattering and cooking utensils rattling far inside, and saw no signs of roasting, boiling or baking around the enormous fireplace, nor copper pans and tin colanders shining on the walls. At one end, however, both light and heat were splendidly reflected by ranks of huge pewter dishes, with silver jugs and tankards between them, rising in row upon row on a vast oak dresser right up to the roof. There was no ceiling beneath that roof: its whole structure lay exposed to an inquisitive eye, except where a wooden rack loaded with oatcakes and bunches of legs of beef, mutton and ham hid it. Above the fireplace hung several evil-looking old guns and a pair of horse pistols; three brightly painted tins arranged on the mantelpiece supplied the decoration. The floor was smooth white stone. The chairs were primitive, high-backed things painted green, with one or two heavy black ones lurking in the shadows. A huge liver-coloured female pointer lay in an arched recess beneath the dresser, surrounded by a swarm of squealing puppies; other dogs occupied the remaining corners.

The room and its furniture would have been perfectly ordinary possessions for a plain northern farmer, a stubborn-faced man whose sturdy legs showed well in knee breeches and gaiters. You may see such a man sitting in his armchair, a mug of frothing ale on the round table before him, anywhere within five or six miles of these hills, if you arrive at the right time after dinner. But Mr. Heathcliff presents a striking contrast to his home and way of life. In appearance he is a dark-skinned gypsy; in clothes and manners, a gentleman—that is, as much of one as many a country squire. He may be somewhat untidy, but his neglect does not look bad on him, for he stands straight and has a handsome figure; and he is rather sullen. Some people might suspect a touch of ill-bred pride. Something sympathetic within me says it is nothing of the kind: I know instinctively that his reserve comes from a dislike of showy feelings—of demonstrations of mutual goodwill. He will conceal his love and hatred equally, and think it something of an impertinence to be loved or hated in return. No, I am getting ahead of myself: I am much too ready to give him my own characteristics. Mr. Heathcliff may have entirely different reasons from mine for keeping his hand out of reach when someone hopes to make his acquaintance. Let me hope that my disposition is almost unique: my dear mother used to say I would never have a comfortable home; and only last summer I proved myself completely unworthy of one.

During a month of fine weather at the seaside, I found myself in the company of a most fascinating creature: a true goddess in my eyes, so long as she took no notice of me. I “never told my love” aloud; yet, if looks can speak, the greatest idiot could have guessed that I was head over heels. At last she understood, and answered with a look—the sweetest look anyone could imagine. And what did I do? I confess it with shame: I withdrew icily into myself, like a snail. With every glance I retreated further and grew colder, until the poor innocent finally began to distrust her own senses and, overwhelmed with embarrassment at her supposed mistake, persuaded her mother to leave.
This curious twist in my character has earned me a reputation for intentional heartlessness. Only I can understand how little I deserve it.

I sat down at the opposite end of the hearth from the one my landlord approached, and tried to fill a silence by stroking the mother dog. She had left her puppies and was creeping wolfishly behind my legs, lip curled, white teeth watering for a bite. My friendly touch brought out a long growl deep in her throat.

“You'd best leave the dog alone,” Mr. Heathcliff growled in accompaniment, stopping her more threatening movements with a thrust of his foot. “She isn't used to being fussed over—we don't keep her as a pet.” Then he strode to a side door and shouted once more, “Joseph!”

From the depths of the cellar Joseph muttered something indistinct, but showed no sign of coming up. His master therefore plunged down after him, leaving me _vis-à-vis_ the ruffianly bitch and two grim, shaggy sheepdogs, who joined her in jealously watching every movement I made. Having no wish to meet their fangs, I kept still; but I imagined they could hardly understand insults delivered in silence, and unfortunately began winking and pulling faces at the three of them. Some twist of my features so offended madam that she flew into a sudden rage and jumped onto my knees. I threw her off and hurried to get the table between us. This action stirred up the whole hive: half a dozen four-legged devils, of different ages and sizes, came out of hidden dens and converged on the same spot. My heels and coat tails seemed particularly singled out for attack; and while I kept the bigger fighters off with the poker as well as I could, I was forced to call loudly for someone in the household to help restore peace.

Mr. Heathcliff and his servant climbed the cellar steps with infuriating calm. I doubt they moved a second faster than usual, although the hearth was a perfect storm of snapping and yelping. Fortunately someone in the kitchen acted more quickly: a vigorous woman with her dress tucked up, her arms bare and her cheeks red from the fire rushed among us brandishing a frying pan. She used this weapon and her tongue so effectively that the storm subsided as if by magic. When her master appeared, she alone remained in motion, heaving like the sea after a gale.
“What the devil is going on?” he demanded, looking me over in a way I could hardly bear after such an inhospitable reception.
“What the devil indeed!” I muttered. “The herd of possessed swine can't have held worse spirits than these animals of yours, sir. You might as well abandon a stranger among a litter of tigers!”
“They leave people alone if people leave things alone,” he observed, setting the bottle in front of me and putting the table back. “Quite right of the dogs to keep watch. A glass of wine?”
“No, thank you.”
“You haven't been bitten?”
“If I had, I'd have left my own mark on the biter.” Heathcliff's face loosened into a grin.

“Come now,” he said, “you're upset, Mr. Lockwood. Here, have a little wine. Visitors are so extraordinarily uncommon in this house that my dogs and I, I'll readily admit, scarcely know how to welcome them. Your health, sir?”

I bowed and drank to his health in return, beginning to see how foolish it would be to sit sulking over the bad behaviour of a pack of mongrels. Besides, since his humour ran that way, I was unwilling to give the fellow any further amusement at my expense. He—probably reflecting sensibly that offending a good tenant would be foolish—relaxed somewhat his clipped manner of speech, with its missing pronouns and helping verbs, and began what he supposed would interest me: a discussion of the merits and drawbacks of my present retreat. He knew a great deal about the subjects we touched on; and by the time I left for home I felt encouraged enough to offer to visit again tomorrow. He clearly had no wish for me to intrude a second time. Nevertheless, I shall go. It is astonishing how sociable I feel when I compare myself with him.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: Yesterday afternoon turned cold and misty. I was half inclined to spend it by the fire in my study, rather than struggle through heather and mud to Wuthering Heights. But when I came upstairs after dinner—note that I dine between twelve and one: the housekeeper, a motherly woman who came with the house as part of its equipment, either could not or would not understand my request to be served at five—when, I say, I went upstairs with this idle plan and entered the room, I found a servant girl kneeling among brushes and coal scuttles, raising a hellish cloud of dust as she smothered the flames with heaps of cinders. The sight drove me straight out again. I took my hat, walked four miles, and reached Heathcliff's garden gate just in time to avoid the first feathery flakes of a snow shower.

Up on that bleak hilltop a dry frost had hardened the ground, and the air sent shivers through every limb. I could not undo the chain, so I climbed over and ran up the paved path between straggling gooseberry bushes. I knocked in vain for someone to let me in, until my knuckles tingled and the dogs began to howl.

“Miserable inhabitants!” I exclaimed inwardly. “For such boorish inhospitality you deserve to be cut off from the human race for ever. At least I would not bar my doors in broad daylight. I don't care—I will get inside!” With this determination I grabbed the latch and shook it violently. Joseph's vinegar face emerged from a round window in the barn.
“What d'ye want?” he shouted. “T' master's down in t' yard. Go round t' end o' t' barn if ye want to speak to him.”
“Isn't there anyone in the house who can open up?” I shouted back.
“There's nobbut t' missis; and she won't open it, though ye make that frightful din till night.”
“Why not? Can't you tell her who I am, Joseph?”
“Not me! I'll have no hand in it,” the head muttered, and disappeared.

The snow began blowing thickly. I caught hold of the handle for another attempt, just as a young man in his shirtsleeves, carrying a pitchfork on his shoulder, appeared in the yard behind me. He called to me to follow him. After going through a washhouse and a paved yard containing a coal shed, a pump and a pigeon house, we finally reached the great warm, welcoming room where I had been received before. It shone delightfully in the light of an enormous fire of coal, peat and wood; and beside a table laid for a generous evening meal I was pleased to see the “missis,” whose existence I had never even suspected. I bowed and waited, expecting her to invite me to sit. Leaning back in her chair, she looked at me without moving or speaking.
“Terrible weather!” I observed. “I'm afraid, Mrs. Heathcliff, your door will have suffered from the leisurely way your servants answer it: I had quite a struggle to make them hear.”
She did not open her mouth. I stared, and she stared too—or at least kept her eyes fixed on me with a cold indifference that was exceedingly unpleasant and embarrassing.
“Take a seat,” the young man said roughly. “He'll be here shortly.”
I did as he said, cleared my throat and called the villain Juno, who on this second meeting graciously moved the very tip of her tail to acknowledge our acquaintance.
“What a fine animal!” I tried again. “Will you be finding homes for the puppies, madam?”
“They don't belong to me,” said my charming hostess, with more hostility than even Heathcliff could have managed.
“Ah, perhaps these are your favourites?” I continued, turning towards a shadowy cushion covered with what looked like cats.
“An odd choice of favourites that would be!” she said contemptuously.
Unfortunately they were a pile of dead rabbits. I cleared my throat again, moved nearer the fire, and repeated my observation about the wild evening.
“You ought to have stayed at home,” she said, getting up and reaching for two of the painted tins on the mantelpiece.

Before, her seat had kept her out of the light; now I could see her entire face and figure clearly. She was slender, and seemed barely past girlhood: a lovely figure, and the most exquisite little face I have ever had the pleasure of seeing. Her features were small and very fair; flaxen curls—or golden, rather—hung loose over her delicate neck. Her eyes, if their expression had been pleasant, would have been irresistible. Fortunately for my easily touched heart, the only feeling they showed lay somewhere between scorn and a sort of despair, strangely out of place in such eyes. The tins were almost beyond her reach; I moved to help, and she turned on me as a miser might turn on someone who offered to help him count his gold.
“I need no help from you,” she snapped. “I can reach them myself.”
“Please forgive me!” I replied hastily.
“Has anyone invited you to tea?” she demanded, fastening an apron over her neat black dress and holding a spoonful of tea leaves above the pot.
“I'd be very glad of a cup,” I replied.
“Have you been invited?” she asked again.
“No,” I answered with half a smile. “That invitation would properly come from you.”
She threw the tea back, spoon and all, and returned to her chair in a sulk, her forehead creased and her red lower lip thrust out like a child's on the verge of tears.

Meanwhile the young man had thrown on an unmistakably shabby coat and stationed himself upright before the fire. He looked down at me out of the corners of his eyes exactly as if some deadly feud between us remained unavenged. I began to wonder whether he was a servant. Both his clothes and his speech were rough, entirely lacking the refinement visible in Mr. and Mrs. Heathcliff. His thick brown curls were untidy and unkempt, his whiskers spread bearishly across his cheeks, and his hands were browned like an ordinary labourer's. Yet his manner was unconstrained, almost proud, and he showed none of a servant's diligence in attending to the lady of the house. With no clear evidence of his position, I thought it best to ignore his strange behaviour. Five minutes later Heathcliff came in, relieving my discomfort to some extent.
“You see, sir, I've kept my promise and come!” I exclaimed, putting on a cheerful manner. “And I'm afraid the weather may keep me here for half an hour, if you can give me shelter for that long.”

“Half an hour?” he said, shaking the white flakes off his clothes. “I'm amazed you chose the middle of a snowstorm for a walk. Do you realise you could lose yourself in the marshes? Even people who know these moors often go astray on evenings like this, and I can tell you there's no prospect of a change just now.”
“Perhaps one of your lads could guide me, and stay at the Grange until morning—could you spare someone?”
“No, I couldn't.”
“Oh, really! Well then, I shall have to rely on my own good sense.”
“Humph!”
“Are ye going to make t' tea?” demanded the wearer of the shabby coat, transferring his ferocious stare from me to the young woman.
“Does _he_ get any?” she asked Heathcliff for a decision.

“Will you get it ready?” he answered, so savagely that I flinched. The way he spoke exposed a truly vicious nature. I no longer felt like calling Heathcliff a splendid fellow. Once everything was prepared, he invited me with, “Now, sir, bring your chair up.” We all drew round the table, the country youth included, and a forbidding silence held while we dealt with our meal.

I thought that if I had brought this cloud over them, I ought to try to clear it. Surely they could not sit in such grim silence every day; however bad-tempered they might be, the scowl on every face could not possibly be their ordinary expression.

“It's curious,” I began, between finishing one cup of tea and receiving the next, “how habit can shape our tastes and ideas. Many people could not imagine happiness in a life as completely cut off from the world as yours, Mr. Heathcliff; yet I venture to say that, surrounded by your family, with your charming wife the guiding spirit of your home and heart—”
“My charming wife!” he interrupted, his face twisted into an almost devilish sneer. “And where is she—my charming wife?”
“I mean Mrs. Heathcliff, your wife.”
“Well, yes—oh, you mean her spirit has become a guardian angel, watching over the fortunes of Wuthering Heights although her body has gone. Is that your meaning?”

Realising I had blundered, I tried to put it right. I might have noticed that the difference in their ages made it unlikely they were husband and wife. One was about forty, an age of mental vigour when men seldom delude themselves that girls marry them for love: that dream is kept to comfort our declining years. The other did not look seventeen.

Then the answer struck me. “That rustic at my elbow, drinking tea from a basin and eating bread with unwashed hands, may be her husband: Heathcliff junior, of course. This is what comes of being buried alive: she has wasted herself on that boor because she simply doesn't know that better men exist! What a pity—I must take care not to make her regret her choice.” That last thought may sound conceited; it was not. The man beside me seemed almost repulsive, while I knew from experience that I was reasonably attractive.

“Mrs. Heathcliff is my daughter-in-law,” Heathcliff said, confirming my guess. As he spoke, he gave her a peculiar look: a look of hatred, unless his facial muscles work in some very perverse way and, unlike other people's, refuse to express what is in his soul.
“Ah, of course—I understand now: you are the fortunate owner of this kindly fairy,” I remarked, turning to the man beside me.

This was worse than my earlier mistake. The youth turned crimson and clenched his fist, looking thoroughly ready to attack me. But he apparently recovered himself a moment later and choked back his anger with a savage curse muttered for my benefit—which, however, I carefully pretended not to hear.

“Your guesses are unfortunate, sir,” my host observed. “Neither of us enjoys the privilege of possessing your good fairy; her husband is dead. I said she was my daughter-in-law, so she must have married my son.”
“And this young gentleman is—”
“Certainly no son of mine.”
Heathcliff smiled once more, as though suggesting he had fathered that bear was rather too audacious a joke.
“I'm Hareton Earnshaw,” the other man growled, “and I'd advise you to treat that name with respect!”
“I haven't shown it any disrespect,” I answered, privately amused at the dignity of his announcement.

He kept his eyes on me longer than I wished to meet them, for fear I might be tempted either to box his ears or to laugh aloud. I began to feel decidedly out of place in this agreeable family gathering. The gloomy atmosphere of their spirits overwhelmed and more than cancelled out the warm comforts surrounding me, and I resolved to think carefully before venturing beneath that roof a third time.

When the business of eating was finished, and nobody offered a word of friendly conversation, I went to a window to inspect the weather. The sight was dismal: darkness falling before its time, and sky and hills merging in one bitter whirl of wind and smothering snow.
“I really don't think I can get home now without someone to guide me,” I could not help exclaiming. “The roads must be buried already; and even if they weren't, I could scarcely see a foot ahead.”
“Hareton, get those twelve sheep under the barn porch. They'll be buried if they're left in the pen all night, and put a plank across in front of them,” Heathcliff said.
“What am I supposed to do?” I persisted, growing irritated.

Nobody answered my question. Looking round, I saw only Joseph carrying in a bucket of porridge for the dogs, and Mrs. Heathcliff bent over the fire, amusing herself by burning a bundle of matches that had fallen from the mantelpiece when she put back the tea tin. Having set his load down, Joseph surveyed the room disapprovingly and rasped in his cracked voice, “I wonder how ye can bring yerself to stand there doing nowt and worse, when all t' others have gone out! But ye're a good-for-nowt, and talking's no use—ye'll never mend yer wicked ways, but go straight to t' devil, like yer mother before ye!”
For a moment I thought this eloquent speech was meant for me. Angry enough, I stepped towards the old rogue with the intention of kicking him out of the door; but Mrs. Heathcliff's reply stopped me.

“You disgraceful old hypocrite!” she answered. “Aren't you afraid of being carried off, body and all, every time you speak the devil's name? Take care how you provoke me, or I'll ask him to abduct you as a particular favour! Wait! Look here, Joseph,” she went on, taking a long, dark book off a shelf. “I'll show you how much I've learned of the Black Art: soon I'll know enough to clear the whole house. That red cow didn't die by accident, and your rheumatism can hardly be put down to the workings of Providence!”
“Oh, wicked, wicked!” the old man gasped. “May t' Lord deliver us from evil!”

“No, sinner! You're already damned—get out, or I'll do you real harm! I'll make images of every one of you in wax and clay! And the first to cross the boundaries I set shall—I won't tell you what will happen to him—but you'll see! Go on, I'm watching you!”

The little witch put a pretence of malice into her lovely eyes. Joseph hurried out trembling with very real horror, praying and exclaiming “wicked” as he went. I supposed she was indulging in some sort of bleak amusement; and now we were alone I tried to interest her in my predicament.

“Mrs. Heathcliff,” I said earnestly, “forgive me for troubling you. I take the liberty because I'm certain someone with your face must be kind-hearted. Please point out some landmarks so I can find my way home: I know no more about getting there than you would about finding your way to London!”
“Go back the way you came,” she replied, settling into a chair with a candle and the long book open before her. “It's short advice, but the best I can offer.”
“So if you hear they've found me dead in a bog or a snow-filled pit, your conscience won't suggest you were partly to blame?”
“Why should it? I can't go with you. They wouldn't let me as far as the end of the garden wall.”
“_You_! I'd be sorry to ask you to step outside for my sake on a night like this,” I cried. “I want you to _tell_ me the way, not _show_ me: or persuade Mr. Heathcliff to let me have a guide.”
“Who? There's him, Earnshaw, Zillah, Joseph and me. Which one do you want?”
“Don't you have any boys working on the farm?”
“No. That's everyone.”
“Then it seems I have no choice but to stay.”
“You'll have to arrange that with your host. It's no concern of mine.”

“I hope this teaches you not to go wandering recklessly over these hills again,” came Heathcliff's harsh voice from the kitchen doorway. “As for staying, I don't provide rooms for visitors: you'll have to share a bed with Hareton or Joseph.”
“A chair in this room would do for me to sleep in,” I replied.
“No, no! Rich or poor, a stranger's still a stranger. It doesn't suit me to let anyone roam about the place when I'm not there to watch!” said the ill-mannered brute.

That insult exhausted my patience. I expressed my disgust and pushed past him into the yard, colliding with Earnshaw in my hurry. It was too dark to see the way out, and as I searched round I heard another example of their courteous behaviour to one another. At first the young man seemed inclined to help me.
“I'll take him as far as the park,” he said.
“You can take him to hell!” exclaimed his master, or whatever he was to him. “And who'll see to the horses, eh?”
“A man's life matters more than leaving the horses for one evening: someone must go,” Mrs. Heathcliff murmured, with more kindness than I had expected.
“Not because you order it!” Hareton shot back. “If you care about him, you'd do better to keep quiet.”
“Then I hope his ghost comes back to haunt you, and I hope Mr. Heathcliff gets no more tenants until the Grange falls to pieces,” she answered sharply.
“Listen, listen, she's putting a curse on 'em!” muttered Joseph, towards whom I had been making my way.
He was sitting within hearing, milking the cows by lantern light. Without ceremony I seized the lantern and, calling out that I would return it tomorrow, rushed towards the nearest small gate.
“Master, master, he's stealing t' lantern!” the old man shouted, chasing after me. “Hey, Gnasher! Hey, dog! Hey, Wolf, hold him, hold him!”

As I opened the little door, two hairy monsters sprang at my throat, knocked me down and put out the light. Heathcliff and Hareton's mingled laughter crowned my fury and humiliation. Fortunately, the animals seemed more interested in stretching their paws, yawning and wagging their tails than in eating me alive; but they would allow no rising from the dead, and I had to lie there until their spiteful masters chose to release me. Then, hatless and shaking with anger, I ordered the villains to let me out, and warned them they kept me another minute at their peril. I added several confused threats of revenge which, in their vague depths of venom, had a flavour of King Lear.

The violence of my agitation brought on a heavy nosebleed; still Heathcliff laughed, and still I raged. I don't know how the scene would have ended if someone rather more sensible than I, and more kindly than my host, had not been nearby. This was Zillah, the stout housekeeper, who finally came out to discover what the commotion meant. She thought some of them had been attacking me, and, not daring to turn on her master, aimed her verbal artillery at the younger scoundrel.

“Well, Mr. Earnshaw,” she cried, “whatever will ye be up to next? Are we to murder folk on our own doorstep? I can see this house'll never suit me—look at t' poor lad, he's fair choking! Hush, hush; ye mustn't carry on so. Come inside and I'll put that right: there now, keep yerself still.”

With that she suddenly poured a pint of ice-cold water down my neck and dragged me into the kitchen. Mr. Heathcliff came after us, his chance burst of amusement quickly fading into his customary sullenness.

I felt terribly sick, dizzy and faint, and so had no choice but to accept a night's lodging under his roof. He told Zillah to give me a glass of brandy, then went through to the inner room. She sympathised with my miserable state and, after obeying his orders—which revived me a little—showed me to bed.
